newsitem.title: UK: LME copper higher ahead of stocks, tin vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: LME copper higher ahead of stocks, tin vulnerable.

text.p: Copper prices rose on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Monday, buoyed by expectations of another drop in stocks on Tuesday, traders and analysts said.
But all base metal markets finished the day below the highs as softening nearby spreads on copper undermined the complex.
"Copper looked set to have a look at $2,000 (a tonne), but the easing spread was the main inhibitive factor," said Robin Bhar, analyst at LME ring dealers Brandeis.
"The nearby rates haven't really moved up, so there does not appear to be too much panic in the market despite stocks being at very low levels," he added.
Three month copper futures finished the afternoon kerb at $1,972 a tonne, up $14 from Friday's close but well below the day's high of $1,985.
LME stocks are at six-year lows of 123,700 tonnes and are forecast to fall another 5,000 to 10,000 tonnes on Tuesday.
But despite expectations of further tightening of nearby copper supplies, spreads eased on Monday with cash narrowing to around $45 above three months from $50 at the close on Friday.
Traders are keeping a close eye on November copper values in the run up to the November options declaration on Wednesday. The key strike prices are $1,950, $2,000 and $2,100, traders said.
The fact that price volatility tends to increase around option declarations is adding to already considerable market uncertainty.
"I wouldn't like to call the next $50 in copper," said Bhar.
Technical support is pegged at $1,925, while resistance is expected to emerge at $1,985/90.
Other base metals finished lower in mostly routine trade, although tin dipped briefly to a 17-month nadir of $5,890 before recovering slightly.
"There was general Far Eastern selling interest on tin, and the charts do not look good," said one trader.
"A break below $5,890/5,900 would see the market looking at $5,600/5,700," Brandeis' Bhar said. The market would remain vulnerable until it recovered back above $6,050, he added.
Tin finished at $5,900, down $75 from Friday's close.
Zinc lost ground, slipping to $1,066 from $1,073.50.
Traders said an overbought market and the lack of follow-through buying from investment funds would limit the market's upside potential in the short term.
But further ahead values were expected to rise, some added.
Nickel fell slightly to $7,160 from $7,190. "The market found good trade and fund buying," a dealer said.
Aluminium held steady despite copper's weakness, ending just $0.50 softer at $1,424.50.
Lead fell $10 to $741 in quiet conditions, while alloy edged up to $1,282/85 from $1,275.
--Mike Collett-White, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8057
